llm_reflection.explanation: Round-005 completed the first probe of G_dual_bottleneck using the bottleneck rule policy. The result is verified: status completed, 4 of 4 wafers released and completed, zero unfinished wafers, independent replay valid, zero constraint violations, zero deadlocks. It establishes the first incumbent for this scenario at makespan 199.0 s, accepted as first_verified_candidate. This is a baseline, not an optimum. The static analysis predicted a nominal bottleneck of CLEAN with CLEAN and RINSE both at 56.0 s nominal load and DRY at 36.0 s, and a zero blocking-to-processing ratio. The measured schedule is far above the 56.0 s nominal lower bound: 199.0 s, about 3.55x the nominal minimum load. Chamber processing seconds match the nominal loads exactly (CLEAN 56.0, RINSE 56.0, DRY 36.0), so the gap is not extra processing; it is waiting and blocking. Robot action time is 151.0 s with robot utilization 0.3775, mean chamber utilization only 0.1233, and total chamber blocking 78.0 s (CLEAN 25.0, RINSE 24.0, DRY 29.0). Wafer waiting is large and grows monotonically by release order: W01 12.0 s, W02 40.0 s, W03 106.0 s, W04 131.0 s, average 72.25 s. This pattern indicates the bottleneck rule policy serializes the batch poorly: later wafers wait progressively longer, so the schedule is dominated by robot transfer serialization and chamber blocking rather than by chamber capacity. The static blocking-to-processing ratio of 0.0 was not predictive of the dynamic behavior; the measured blocking_rate is 0.065 and blocking is substantial. This is consistent with the F_competition finding that makespan there was dominated by robot serialization and blocking rather than raw chamber load. It also falsifies the optimistic branch of the prior hypothesis that a close-to-nominal baseline would indicate chamber capacity dominates; instead the baseline is far above nominal, indicating robot serialization dominates on G_dual_bottleneck as well under this rule. Cost was negligible: about 0.41 s wall and 0.046 s skill time, so this was a high-value probe. The next question is whether the 199.0 s baseline is near the best achievable or whether a stronger method can substantially reduce it. CP-SAT is the natural next test because it can optimize transfer ordering and blocking jointly, and the untried CP budget for this scenario is 1 s (estimated about 4 s wall), which is cheap relative to the remaining wall budget of about 547 s and the remaining CP search budget of 56 s. A 1 s CP run tests whether the rule baseline is far from optimal and whether the solver can find a verified complete-batch schedule below 199.0 s. If CP-SAT at 1 s already improves substantially, that would indicate the rule policy is the limiting factor and that further CP budget is worth spending; if it does not improve, that would suggest the instance is hard for the current encoding or that 199.0 s is closer to the practical limit for these methods.

The only sense in which it underperformed is relative to the static nominal lower bound: the verified makespan of 199.0 s is about 3.55x the 56.0 s nominal minimum load, and the prior hypothesis anticipated that a baseline close to nominal would indicate chamber capacity dominates. That branch was falsified. The static blocking-to-processing ratio of 0.0 was not a reliable predictor of dynamic blocking. This is a meaningful negative result about the rule policy, not about the simulator or verification.
